title: New Jersey's Samudhra Restaurant Signs 10,000-Square-Foot Lease for NYC Debut in Hell's Kitchen
excerpt: The Franklin Park Indian restaurant and lounge is bringing its premium dining concept to The Ellery at 312 West 43rd Street, making one of the largest real estate bets by an Indian restaurant in Manhattan.
body:
• Samudhra, an Indian restaurant and lounge based in Franklin Park, New Jersey, has signed a 10,000-square-foot ground-floor lease at The Ellery, 312 West 43rd Street in Hell's Kitchen
  • The deal represents one of the largest real estate commitments by an Indian restaurant in Manhattan, at a corridor where asking rents average $1,400 per square foot
  • Founder Mangesh Chinthamaneni, a former IT entrepreneur who transitioned into hospitality, is positioning Samudhra as a premium Indian dining and lounge experience
  • The expansion comes amid a broader wave of ambitious Indian dining in New York, led by acclaimed groups like Unapologetic Foods (Semma, Dhamaka, Adda)

A Big Bet on Indian Dining in Manhattan

A New Jersey Indian restaurant is making the leap across the Hudson River with an unusually ambitious real estate play. Samudhra, the Indian restaurant and lounge based in Franklin Park, New Jersey, has signed a 10,000-square-foot lease on the ground floor of The Ellery at 312 West 43rd Street in Hell's Kitchen, marking the concept's first Manhattan location.

The deal, announced by building owners Taconic Partners and National Real Estate Advisors, places Samudhra in a premium Midtown corridor near Times Square where ground-floor asking rents averaged $1,400 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. At that rate, the lease represents a significant financial commitment that dwarfs the footprints of most Indian restaurants currently operating in Manhattan.

"The Ellery provides an exceptional setting for our New York City location and gives us the opportunity to introduce our distinctive premium Indian dining and lounge experience to a much broader audience."

— Mangesh Chinthamaneni, Founder and CEO, Samudhra

From IT to Hospitality

Samudhra's founder, Mangesh Chinthamaneni, took an unconventional path to the restaurant business. A former IT entrepreneur, Chinthamaneni moved into hospitality to build what he describes as a premium Indian dining and lounge experience. The Franklin Park restaurant, Samudhra's first US location, established a following in central New Jersey before Chinthamaneni set his sights on Manhattan.

The name Samudhra derives from the Sanskrit word for ocean, reflecting the restaurant's ambition to offer a broad and immersive culinary experience rather than a narrow regional focus.

A Different Scale Entirely

What makes Samudhra's move notable is not just the location but the sheer scale. Manhattan has seen a genuine and well-documented wave of ambitious Indian dining in recent years, but the restaurants driving that wave have overwhelmingly chosen smaller, more intimate footprints.

Unapologetic Foods, the hospitality group behind Adda, Dhamaka, and Semma, has grown from a single 2017 restaurant into seven concepts across Manhattan and Brooklyn. Semma, the group's South Indian concept, earned a Michelin star and topped The New York Times' list of the 100 best restaurants in New York City in 2025. Chef Vikas Khanna and restaurateur Jimmy Rizvi opened Bungalow in the East Village in 2024 as another high-profile entry. But Semma seats 79 people. Dhamaka operates inside Essex Market. These are critically important restaurants that have reshaped how Indian food is perceived in New York, but they operate at a fraction of Samudhra's planned scale.

At 10,000 square feet in a corridor commanding some of the highest retail rents in the city, Samudhra's commitment is closer to how a national chain or an already-scaled hospitality group might approach Manhattan than how the city's most celebrated Indian restaurants have grown.

Why Times Square, Why Now

The choice of corridor may be as strategic as it is ambitious. According to REBNY's first-half 2026 Manhattan retail report, neighborhoods like SoHo and Madison Avenue have been squeezed to fewer than 20 available storefronts combined. Times Square and the surrounding Midtown West area, by contrast, still carry elevated vacancy from the pandemic's impact on tourism-dependent retail, which means more available large-format space and rents that remain negotiable relative to the city's tightest submarkets.

The Ellery itself has been a successful mixed-use development. The building filled all 330 of its apartments within 11 months of launching leasing in mid-2024, and German grocery chain Aldi signed a 25,000-square-foot ground-floor lease at the property roughly a year before Samudhra's deal.

What It Means for Indian Dining in America

For Indian Americans and the broader diaspora community, Samudhra's move carries symbolic weight. Indian restaurants in Manhattan have historically occupied modest storefronts on Lexington Avenue's Curry Hill or intimate neighborhood spots in the East Village. The new wave led by Unapologetic Foods has elevated the cuisine's critical standing, but the real estate footprints have remained small. Samudhra's bet — that an Indian restaurant concept can sustain a flagship-scale presence in a premium Manhattan corridor — tests whether the cuisine's rising cultural cachet can translate into the kind of commercial scale that other global cuisines achieved in New York long ago.

CBRE's Lon Rubackin, Michael Kadosh, and Bevan Cohen negotiated on behalf of the landlord, while Brad Schwarz from Lee & Associates represented Samudhra. An opening date has not been announced.
